issues.legal_issue: A magistrate who receives a police-recorded confession for onward transmission is not required to independently reassess its voluntariness unless the accused raises a grievance.
material_facts: The accused were produced before a magistrate with sealed police-recorded confessions for transmission to the designated court.
The accused made no complaint of harassment, torture, or coercion before the magistrate.
The magistrate forwarded the confessions to the designated court.
issues.conclusion: The magistrate was not required to reopen the confessions or independently certify their voluntariness; the trial court erred in excluding them on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987 and Rule 15(5) of the Rules require the recorded confession to be sent through the designated magistrate to the designated court; they do not require the magistrate to open the sealed confession or reassess voluntariness. Under Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, the magistrate must record any statement or complaint the accused makes and arrange a medical examination if torture is alleged, but need not record the confession afresh or inquire into its circumstances absent such a complaint.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The matter came before the court in an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.police_recorded_confession_sent_to_magis: A police officer recorded a confession and sent it through a magistrate for onward transmission to the trial court.
predicates.accused_made_no_grievance: The accused raised no complaint of coercion, torture, or other mistreatment before the magistrate.

issues.definition: When a police-recorded confession is sent through a magistrate and the accused raises no grievance there, the magistrate need not reassess its voluntariness.

issues.legal_issue: A police-recorded confession remains admissible despite an omitted prescribed memorandum or other alleged recording irregularities when the confession was voluntary and the recording requirements were substantially followed.
material_facts: The police officer questioned each accused about whether the confession was voluntary, warned that making a confession was not compulsory, and allowed time before recording the statement.
The officer testified that each confession was voluntary and denied that the statements had been altered or ante-dated.
The officer omitted the memorandum specified in the rules, but complied with the other recording requirements and the safeguards described by the court.
The trial court excluded the confessions based on the omitted memorandum, the timing of their transmission, and apparent differences in the typewritten text.
issues.conclusion: The confessions were voluntarily made and legally recorded; the trial court erred in excluding them, and they were admissible in evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987 and Rule 15 of the Rules govern police-recorded confessions. Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab sets safeguards for recording such confessions. A failure to reproduce the prescribed memorandum does not automatically invalidate a confession where the officer’s evidence establishes voluntariness and the requirements have otherwise been substantially met. Sharafathussain Abdulrahaman Shaikh v. State of Gujarat is distinguishable where the recording officer did not testify to his satisfaction that the confession was voluntary.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and police_confession_recorded and confession_voluntary and recording_requirements_substantially_followed and officer_testified_to_voluntariness

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The matter came before the court in an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.police_confession_recorded: A police officer recorded the accused's confession.
predicates.confession_voluntary: The accused made the confession of their own free will, without threat, inducement, or pressure.
predicates.recording_requirements_substantially_fol: The recording officer followed the applicable safeguards in substance, although a prescribed formality was omitted.
predicates.officer_testified_to_voluntariness: The recording officer testified that the confession was voluntary.

issues.definition: A voluntary police-recorded confession is admissible when the recording safeguards were substantially followed and the recording officer testified to its voluntariness, even if a prescribed formality was omitted.

issues.legal_issue: A voluntary and legally recorded confession that is generally corroborated may support conviction despite being retracted.
material_facts: The accused later retracted their confessions, which the court found had been made voluntarily and legally recorded.
The confessions described the accused's participation in the attack, their associates, the planning and execution of the crime, and their contacts with criminal leaders.

Other evidence generally corroborated the confessions, including evidence placing the accused near the crime, their association with the other participants, weapon recoveries, identification evidence, and testimony concerning the motive.
issues.conclusion: The confessions were sufficiently corroborated and could support conviction; the trial court erred in rejecting them, and the accused were convicted of the charged offences.
issues.legal_principle: A retracted confession may be relied on if it was voluntary and lawful. Corroboration is a rule of prudence, not a rule of law, and general corroboration may suffice depending on the circumstances. Under Section 15 of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, a qualifying confession is substantive evidence against its maker and may also be used against a co-accused. The court relied on S.N. Dube v. N.B. Bhoir, State v. Nalini, Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, and the treatment of corroboration in the authorities discussed in those cases.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and confession_voluntary and confession_legally_recorded and confession_retracted and confession_generally_corroborated

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The matter came before the court in an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.confession_voluntary: The accused made the confession of their own free will, without threat, inducement, or pressure.
predicates.confession_legally_recorded: The confession was recorded in accordance with the applicable legal safeguards.
predicates.confession_retracted: The accused later withdrew or denied the confession.
predicates.confession_generally_corroborated: Other evidence supported the confession in material respects.

issues.definition: A retracted confession that was voluntary, lawfully recorded, and generally corroborated may support a conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal conviction for conspiracy and related offences cannot rest on unreliable evidence of threats and an unproved connection between the accused and the perpetrators.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that two accused participated in a conspiracy to murder a businessman and attempt to murder his brother.
The alleged threats in a meeting were not mentioned in the witness's police statement, and the investigating officer confirmed the omission; the court treated it as a material contradiction.
The evidence did not establish that the accused had secured the services of, or were connected to, the alleged organizers and perpetrators of the killing.
One accused's conduct as a solicitor could be unprofessional but was not, without more, criminal; no overt or covert criminal act was attributed to the other accused.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not prove the accused's participation in the charged crimes or another crime, and their acquittals were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; suspicion, however strong, is not proof. Under Section 145 of the Evidence Act and Section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a prior statement may be used for contradiction, and a material omission may amount to a contradiction when the omission is inconsistent with what the witness later asserts. The court relied on Tahsildar Singh v. State of U.P. and held that professional impropriety alone did not establish criminal liability.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and alleged_conspiracy_unproved and key_threat_evidence_materially_contradicted and no_independent_criminal_act_proved

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The matter came before the court in an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.alleged_conspiracy_unproved: The evidence did not establish a connection between the accused and the alleged perpetrators or organizers of the crime.
predicates.key_threat_evidence_materially_contradic: A witness's account of an important threat was absent from the earlier police statement, and the omission materially undermined the later account.
predicates.no_independent_criminal_act_proved: The evidence established no independent act by the accused that constituted a crime.

issues.definition: An acquittal is upheld when an alleged conspiracy remains unproved, important threat evidence is materially contradicted, and no independent criminal act is established.

issues.legal_issue: An accused charged with a major offence may be convicted of a cognate minor offence proved by the facts when the change does not cause a failure of justice.
material_facts: The accused was charged with murder in connection with a property transaction.
The evidence established that he procured a broker's services and shared the intention to put the owners in fear of injury so as dishonestly to induce them to transfer valuable property.
The evidence did not prove his participation in the murder conspiracy, but the extortion was connected to the transaction underlying the major charge.
The court found that conviction for extortion would not cause a failure of justice.
issues.conclusion: The accused was convicted of extortion with common intention, although he had not been separately charged with that minor offence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 222(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits conviction for a minor offence where the proved facts reduce the charged offence to that minor offence. The offences must be cognate, with common main ingredients, and the alteration must not cause a failure of justice. The court relied on Shamnsaheb M. Multani v. State of Karnataka and Lakhjit Singh v. State of Punjab.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and major_offence_charged and facts_prove_cognate_minor_offence and minor_offence_connected_to_charged_transaction and no_failure_of_justice

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The matter came before the court in an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.major_offence_charged: The accused was charged with a major offence comprising multiple particulars.
predicates.facts_prove_cognate_minor_offence: The facts proved the elements of a lesser offence sharing the main ingredients of the charged offence.
predicates.minor_offence_connected_to_charged_trans: The lesser offence arose from the same transaction or conduct underlying the major charge.
predicates.no_failure_of_justice: Convicting the accused of the lesser offence would not unfairly prejudice the defence or otherwise cause a failure of justice.

issues.definition: A proved cognate lesser offence may support conviction even if not separately charged when it arises from the charged transaction and the conviction causes no failure of justice.

issues.legal_issue: Life imprisonment rather than a death sentence is appropriate when the murder does not qualify as a rarest-of-the-rare case and the offenders were misled youths.
material_facts: The accused were convicted of murder and related offences based on their participation in the killing.
The court considered them misled youths and found that the case did not warrant the maximum penalty.
issues.conclusion: The accused were sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder, without separate sentences for the other offences.
issues.legal_principle: The death penalty is reserved for the rarest of the rare cases; the court concluded that this case did not meet that standard and that the offenders' status as misled youths weighed against the maximum penalty.

predicates.conviction_for_murder: The accused were convicted of murder.
predicates.offenders_were_misled_youths: The court found that the offenders were young people who had been misled.
predicates.case_not_rarest_of_rare: The court found that the circumstances did not make the case one of the rarest of the rare.

issues.definition: When convicted murderers were misled youths and the case is not among the rarest of the rare, life imprisonment is imposed.
